_comment: A worked example and a self-test for scripts/mutate.py.
It mutates worker/ffmpeg_utils.h264_args, which is a good demonstration target for the reason
the whole technique exists here: getting these flags wrong does not raise. A missing -pix_fmt
produces a file that plays fine for the person who made it and is rejected by half the
platforms it is uploaded to, so the only thing between that and a release is a test that
fails. Three of these flags were in fact missing from all seven encode call sites once.
Note the `command`: it points at tests/test_output_compat.py, not tests/test_ffmpeg_utils.py.
The latter covers subprocess timeouts and passes happily with every compatibility flag
removed - which is worth knowing, because pointing a mutation run at the wrong test file
produces a page of escapes that look like missing coverage and are actually a wrong command.
Add a spec per feature batch, next to its tests. Keep each mutation SMALL - one flag, one
comparison, one constant - because a large mutation that gets caught tells you nothing about
which part of it was noticed.

mutations.name: drop_pix_fmt
mutations.why: without -pix_fmt yuv420p the encode succeeds and the file is rejected on upload; nothing in the pipeline can see it

mutations.name: wrong_profile
mutations.why: the profile is part of the compatibility contract, and a wrong one still encodes

mutations.name: fps_normalisation_always_on
mutations.why: an intermediate about to be re-encoded must not be resampled twice, so this has to stay opt-in

mutations.name: reorder_the_compat_flags
mutations.why: declared equivalent: ffmpeg does not care about the order of these three, and the test checks each flag and its value rather than the sequence - so this SHOULD escape. Included to show what a legitimate `equivalent: true` looks like: the mutation changes the source and provably nothing observable. Use it sparingly, and never to silence an escape you have not understood.
